response.title: A Garden That Could Wait
response.passage:
At Oak Hill High, the science club cared for a small garden beside the cafeteria. Students watered it from an outdoor tap, but they noticed that the tap sometimes ran weakly after several dry days. The garden’s new seedlings needed steady care, and the club wanted a way to keep them alive without using as much tap water. This shortage had become especially clear during the previous month’s dry week, when the garden beds began to crack. The head custodian explained that the school could collect rainwater, but only if the students stored it safely and followed the school’s rules.

The club made a plan before the next storm. One group measured the roof area and estimated how much rain the gutters might collect, while another checked which containers had tight lids. They also decided to reserve two covered containers for seedlings they would plant later in the term. The containers would stay empty until the garden’s next planting day, so the club could keep its promise without taking water away from the plants that already needed it. Students then asked the principal to confirm the school’s policy before they set anything up.

The current school rule allowed collected rainwater to be used on plants, but not for washing tools or filling bottles. That limit meant the club had to keep the storage area separate from the drinking fountains and label each container clearly. The custodian helped them connect a clean barrel to one downspout and showed them how to check its lid after windy weather. After the first storm, the students measured the water and recorded the date, rainfall, and amount collected. They used some of it on the garden and left the two reserved containers untouched.

For several weeks, the club compared its records with the weather and the garden’s condition. On dry days, the stored water kept the older plants from wilting, while the reserved supply remained ready for the later seedlings. The students did not claim that one barrel could solve every water problem at school. Instead, their dated chart showed how much rain the roof could provide and when the garden needed it most. At the end of the term, they shared the results with the principal and suggested adding a second barrel if the school approved the cost. Their small project gave the next group of students a clear plan to build on.
